members of the aviation system here in New Zealand.

Regions and Transport.
So that council

of those is consumer information
in the event of delays and cancellations and that sort of thing.
And
the Aviation Action Plan is publicly available, and the
action relevant to that matter is in that
action plan.
And the publicly available information tells us that
officials have taken advice to Minister Shaw on this matter.
And in fact, in very recent days,
officials have been talking to airlines about a voluntary customer
charter to address some of these challenges
in a way that would improve outcomes for consumers.

Shaw, and
allow that work to continue as it should, rather than
adding another process that might be duplicitous
on this matter.
Duplicitous, I don't think

Yes.

the twain meet.

I'll come in.
The first thing is
the compensation that you get if you
have a delay on an international flight under Montreal
versus what you get paid out domestically,
are they aligned?
Because often in airports you sort of get the $10 voucher, go and have a cup of
coffee type stuff if you are delayed.
What is the sort of level of compensation, and is that standard across the
airlines?
So the Montreal Convention is
something that airlines have to comply with on their
global networks and, of course, here in New Zealand.
And I don't profess to be an aviation lawyer, so I would
not like to
say exactly how it works.
But I think
here in New Zealand, and in line with the Montreal Convention, we talk
about
matters that are within and outside of the airline's control.
So if there is a weather event, for example, that is outside of the airline's
control and generally does not attract, for example,
compensation to the passenger. What airlines
will do is they will re-accommodate that passenger on the next available service if
they can and that sort of thing. And we've seen a lot of that,
for example, when Auckland Airport flooded substantially,
airlines worked really hard to re-accommodate those passengers even where they
might not have had to. So I think airlines will go above
sometimes what international conventions will otherwise dictate.
Okay. So the question of the timing, and you raise it twice in your
report, and you do list them,
there are clearly issues that the airline
is responsible for.
Yes.
You
don't have a crew turn up. You have an engine breakdown.
Those
you don't have to wait. And you talk about having to
come to a firm view on where liability
sits for a delay. Where it's evident and obvious
that it is the airline, for instance, as opposed to
someone on a ground handling service whacking into the side of the
plane. It happened in Wellington once with me.
At that situation, do airlines automatically pay
out and compensate and make people aware?
Or that's where I think the way you wrote
your report, it was very unclear about when there was clear liability
and people were sitting in the airport as opposed to, oh, well, I don't know,
if it's fog related or something like that, then that's a different issue, right?
Is it-
I think that
when the matter is within the airline's control, the most important thing that the
airline is going to try and do immediately is actually get the customer
where they wish to go. So they won't, for example,
refund the customer and leave them stranded wherever they are and let them go off
and buy a new ticket because that isn't getting the customer the service that they
actually want, which is the travel.
So in the first instance, airlines will do all they can to get the
customer where they need to go as soon as possible.
And where that's not possible, and the delay or the disruption is within the
airline's control, then that is something that airlines
will give the customer options for refund or credit
or travel on another service. Those other options
then roll out. But the first thing is always, can we get the customer where they
want to go?
All right. Thank you.
All right. See you there. Greg Fleming, sorry.

charter is going to be adhered to?

make quick progress

frameworks emerging around the world, and they are
generating very sort of perverse and
unintended outcomes with a lot more delay and difficulty in
progressing complaints. And I think that actually if we wanted
to have a sort of sensible run at this,
having a voluntary charter is a great first step.
And then if that
is not working, then we can look at more difficult
and frankly more costly solutions.
But actually, this is a really sensible first step.

make it clear to the airlines that
what you just outlined is the process-

Yeah.

here. I've not had great problems in this country.

90 minutes,
they're

the communication can't always be acknowledging

talking about,
Celie, with your delay.
